result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.min_weighted_vertex_cover()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find a vertex cover of small total weight (2-approximation). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L58413-L58487){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.min_weighted_vertex_cover(weight_attr=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Minimum weighted vertex cover](/assets/graphs/min-weighted-vertex-cover.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A star: a hub joined to four leaves a, b, c, d, with node costs in badges, 10 for the hub and 1 for each leaf. Covering every edge with the hub alone costs 10, so the method takes the four leaves instead, in the accent color. The card shows the cover [a, b, c, d] and its cost 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4, against 10 for the hub." width="100%"} A vertex cover is a set of nodes that touches every edge. With node weights (costs), the goal is a cover of minimum total weight, such as the cheapest set of servers that monitors every link, or the fewest guards who together watch every corridor. That problem is NP-hard, so this method returns a cover that is guaranteed to weigh at most twice the optimum, and is often much closer. Without weights it minimizes the number of nodes (with the same guarantee). On bipartite graphs, `bipartite_vertex_cover()` finds an exact minimum (unweighted). Edge direction is ignored. A self-loop forces its node into the cover. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weight_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of a node attribute holding non-negative costs. If `None` (default), every node costs `1`. Nodes without the attribute, or with a non-numeric value, cost `1`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node IDs of the cover, in ascending order. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a node cost is negative or NaN. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} This is the local-ratio algorithm of Bar-Yehuda and Even (1985), as in NetworkX. It scans the edges (in ID order); for each edge not yet covered, it adds the cheaper endpoint to the cover and subtracts that endpoint's remaining cost from the other endpoint. The amounts subtracted form a feasible dual solution that the cover weighs at most twice, which gives the factor-2 guarantee. It runs in $O(V + E)$ time. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A star with a costly center: covering every edge with the center costs 10, while the four cheap leaves cost 4 together, and the method finds that cheaper cover: ::: {#1a1cbe9c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["hub", "a", "b", "c", "d"]) g.add_edges([("hub", "a"), ("hub", "b"), ("hub", "c"), ("hub", "d")]) g.set_node_attrs("cost", {g.get_id_from_label("hub"): 10.0}) cover = g.min_weighted_vertex_cover(weight_attr="cost") [g.get_label_from_id(n) for n in cover] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'] ``` ::: ::: Without costs, the single center node is the smallest cover: ::: {#9f630531 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} [g.get_label_from_id(n) for n in g.min_weighted_vertex_cover()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['hub'] ``` ::: :::
